html:
The Jōmon period was the long age of Japanese prehistory, from about 14,000 to 300 BCE, when the islands were home to foragers who made some of the oldest pottery in the world. The name means "cord-marked", after the patterns pressed into their pots with twisted cord.

The Jōmon people lived mainly by hunting, fishing and gathering: deer and boar, fish and shellfish, nuts such as chestnuts and acorns. The islands were rich enough that many of them settled in villages for long periods, something rare among foragers. At Sannai-Maruyama in northern Honshu, a large village lasted for about 1,500 years, with big wooden buildings and huge piles of shells and waste.

What they left:

  • Jōmon pottery, from plain early pots to the wild "flame" vessels of the middle period
  • clay figures called dogū, often of women with large eyes
  • lacquerware, stone circles, and tools of bone, antler and shell

The chart shows them from 3300 BCE, when the chart starts, but by then they had already lived this way for ten thousand years.

Some cultivation took place, and rice farming may have begun in northern Kyushu as early as about 900 BCE. From then on, migrants from the Korean peninsula brought wet-rice farming and metal. Over the Yayoi period the newcomers and the Jōmon mixed; most modern Japanese carry ancestry from both. Jōmon ancestry survived most strongly in the north, among the Ainu, and in the Ryukyu islands. In the far north a late Jōmon way of life lasted longest.
